Riemann's Rearrangement Theorem

Can rearranging alone manufacture any sum we want?

The greedy rule is simple. Below the target, take a positive term; above it, take a negative one. The terms shrink, so each overshoot shrinks too. That is why any real target can be hit exactly.

For example, think of steering a 🚗 car. Turn more when short of the spot, back when past it. Small corrections land you exactly where you aim.

∑an converges conditionally ⟹ ∀ s∈R  ∃ rearrangement with sum s\sum a_n\ \text{converges conditionally}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\, s\in\mathbb{R}\ \ \exists\ \text{rearrangement with sum } s∑an​ converges conditionally ⟹ ∀s∈R  ∃ rearrangement with sum s

Let ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ be a real series converging conditionally.

∑pn<∞ ⟹ ∑qn=∑pn−∑an<∞ ⟹ ∑∣an∣<∞(contradiction)\sum p_n < \infty \ \Longrightarrow\ \sum q_n = \sum p_n - \sum a_n < \infty \ \Longrightarrow\ \sum \lvert a_n \rvert < \infty \quad \text{(contradiction)}∑pn​<∞ ⟹ ∑qn​=∑pn​−∑an​<∞ ⟹ ∑∣an​∣<∞(contradiction)
Show proof

  1. Termwise an=pn−qna_n = p_n - q_nan​=pn​−qn​ and ∣an∣=pn+qn\lvert a_n \rvert = p_n + q_n∣an​∣=pn​+qn​ (zero terms contribute nothing, so this is the positive/negative subsequences re-indexed). Conditional convergence means ∑(pn−qn)\sum (p_n - q_n)∑(pn​−qn​) converges while ∑(pn+qn)\sum (p_n + q_n)∑(pn​+qn​) diverges.

  2. Suppose ∑pn<∞\sum p_n < \infty∑pn​<∞. Since ∑an=∑(pn−qn)\sum a_n = \sum (p_n - q_n)∑an​=∑(pn​−qn​) converges, and qn=pn−(pn−qn)q_n = p_n - (p_n - q_n)qn​=pn​−(pn​−qn​), the series ∑qn=∑pn−∑an\sum q_n = \sum p_n - \sum a_n∑qn​=∑pn​−∑an​ converges as a difference of convergent series.

  3. Then ∑∣an∣=∑pn+∑qn<∞\sum \lvert a_n \rvert = \sum p_n + \sum q_n < \infty∑∣an​∣=∑pn​+∑qn​<∞ — so ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ would converge absolutely, contradicting conditional convergence. Hence ∑pn=+∞\sum p_n = +\infty∑pn​=+∞.

  4. Symmetrically: if ∑qn<∞\sum q_n < \infty∑qn​<∞, then pn=qn+(pn−qn)p_n = q_n + (p_n - q_n)pn​=qn​+(pn​−qn​) gives ∑pn=∑qn+∑an\sum p_n = \sum q_n + \sum a_n∑pn​=∑qn​+∑an​ convergent, again forcing ∑∣an∣<∞\sum \lvert a_n \rvert < \infty∑∣an​∣<∞ — contradiction.

    So ∑qn=+∞\sum q_n = +\infty∑qn​=+∞.

    The intuition: a conditionally convergent series harbors both "positive infinity" and "negative infinity", and a rearrangement can shuttle between them to hit any target.

Show proof

  1. The alternating harmonic series ∑(−1)n+1n\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}∑n(−1)n+1​ converges conditionally (Leibniz gives convergence; ∑1n\sum \frac1n∑n1​ diverges, so no absolute convergence). For the positive terms pk=12k−1p_k = \frac{1}{2k-1}pk​=2k−11​ and negative magnitudes qk=12kq_k = \frac{1}{2k}qk​=2k1​, we have ∑pk=∑qk=+∞\sum p_k = \sum q_k = +\infty∑pk​=∑qk​=+∞ (a corollary of the previous problem, or directly via 12k−1≥12k\frac{1}{2k-1} \ge \frac{1}{2k}2k−11​≥2k1​ and comparison with the harmonic series).

  2. Both blocks recur forever.

    If positives were taken only finitely often, then eventually only negatives are taken: the running sum drops by qjq_jqj​ each step and ∑qj=∞\sum q_j = \infty∑qj​=∞ forces t→−∞t \to -\inftyt→−∞ — eventually t≤st \le st≤s, and the rule would take a positive: contradiction.

    Symmetrically for negatives (otherwise t→+∞t \to +\inftyt→+∞ would force a negative take).

    Since each block consumes the next unused terms in order, every pip_ipi​ and every qjq_jqj​ is eventually used exactly once — a genuine rearrangement.

  3. Crossing lemma: crossing upward from t≤st \le st≤s by adding ppp, the new gap is (t+p)−s=p−(s−t)≤p(t + p) - s = p - (s - t) \le p(t+p)−s=p−(s−t)≤p (equality only when t=st = st=s).

    Crossing downward from t>st > st>s by subtracting qqq, the new gap is s−(t−q)=q−(t−s)<qs - (t - q) = q - (t - s) < qs−(t−q)=q−(t−s)<q.

    So every crossing overshoot/undershoot is at most its crossing term's magnitude.

  4. Now look at one positive block (after the first crossing; finitely many initial steps don't affect convergence).

    Starting from an undershoot gap ε\varepsilonε (with ε≤qlast\varepsilon \le q_{\text{last}}ε≤qlast​, the last negative taken, by the lemma), the block increases monotonically, so before the crossing step s−S≤εs - S \le \varepsilons−S≤ε, and at the crossing step S−s≤pcrossS - s \le p_{\text{cross}}S−s≤pcross​.

    Hence throughout the block ∣SN−s∣≤max⁡(qlast,pcross)\lvert S_N - s \rvert \le \max(q_{\text{last}}, p_{\text{cross}})∣SN​−s∣≤max(qlast​,pcross​).

  5. Since the blocks recur forever (step 2), both term indices tend to ∞\infty∞: qlast→0q_{\text{last}} \to 0qlast​→0 and pcross→0p_{\text{cross}} \to 0pcross​→0 (the crossing positives are a subsequence of the pip_ipi​).

    Hence ∣SN−s∣→0\lvert S_N - s \rvert \to 0∣SN​−s∣→0, i.e. SN→sS_N \to sSN​→s.

    Negative blocks are symmetric.

    This is the greedy proof of Riemann's rearrangement theorem for finite sss.

    (The ±∞\pm\infty±∞ cases lie outside this statement's scope and need a separate construction: for target +∞+\infty+∞, for instance, replace the fixed target sss by stage targets m→+∞m \to +\inftym→+∞ — at stage mmm, take positive terms until the partial sum exceeds mmm.)
